Just...wow. Advice for anyone who wants to make the best of this game; [u]do not save scum on your first playthrough.[/u] 
The impact of everything will be lost if your actions are without consequences. 

At first I was expecting Orwell to be about the evils of Big Data, huge data mining operations keeping tabs on everyone and everything, but as you play you realize it's much deeper than that. 

First episode there's a joke between friends and the game lets you [spoiler]update the suspects profile to say that she tortures people [/spoiler]. It seems like a joke at first but then you realize: the system doesn't [i]know[/i] it's a joke. Only your presence and understanding of the situation could prevent someone potentially being incacerated for [spoiler] being a crappy baker [/spoiler]... But surely that would never happen right? So long as there are people to check everything it'll all turn out okay won't it?

Then the conflicts come in. Working or creating an alibi? Patriot or Insergent? People will die if you make the wrong call. But you are human. You are fallable. You make mistakes. That is the point of this game. This for me was the message of Orwell. It's not so much about the evils of Big Data, but the dangers of incomplete information. 

In the ideal world of perfect information (an assumption used for the creation of economic models), Orwell and other Big Data operations could be forces for good. However, we do not have perfect information. Imperfection leads to ambiguity, ambiguity leads to assumptions, assumptions lead to mistakes and mistakes lead to suffering. 

I highly recommend the game. My only critique is that the trailer spoils one of the twists. It's a fairly obvious twist, and the trailer would be far worse off had it been left out, but it's worth noting none the less.

I've been meaning to replay this game and see the other endings, but I'd be making choices based on future knowledge rather than the information that's provided to me. While I could spend the time scouring the information we have to find justification for the right call, it's just not the same as it was when that was all you had to go on.
A well-implemented, absorbing, and thought-provoking story-driven game where your decisions can lead to unintended consequences.

So, Orwell is mixture of good stuff and mediocre stuff. I really like the gameplay, structuring and pacing (both of the plot and the gameplay). The central gameplay loop is basically just looking through various documents and conversations to find information potentially relevant to the investigation. I thought it would be boring at first, but it actually never felt tired, and remains engaging throughout. Gameplay wise, it's pretty good, with only a few minor tweaks that could improve efficiency. The story is where it gets less positive. As you progress through the game, you learn more about the characters, who they are, their background, their personality, etc. etc. This is the strongest aspect of the story, because their well written characters, and seeing them react to what's happening after learning so much about them makes you think really carefully about what you do that might affect them. Unfortunately, these characters all seem fixated on the agenda of beating the message of the game over your head repeatedly. The themes and message? That's where we really start to lose traction. First off, the message is obvious. One of the characters at the end practically spells it out. Thanks, if the all the references to the number 1984 didn't make it obvious, nor the chapters being named after phrases from 1984, then I would of still gotten it from the name and premise. Mass surveillance is bad! Like, really unethical! No, really? I thought that was obvious. For the all the 1984 references though, it doesn't seem like the writers really understood 1984. 1984 isn't about surveillance. It's about the manipulation of thought, primarily through language and media. The surveillance is window dressing. In fact, you never even know if the citizens in 1984 are actually being watched, because it doesn't matter. It just matters that they think they are. I digress. The game also comes as thinking it's a bit smarter than it really is. Despite that, it's never boring, and though a little melodramatic, and the tendency to believe that the player hasn't caught on that mass surveillance is kinda screwed up, I did feel desire to continue, and though the end is also a little silly (It forces you to choose between 3 equally culpable people, for no explained reason. Why can't I incriminate them all?), I didn't feel cheated. I didn't pay I got it for free from humble, but I wouldn't have regretted paying for it. Try episode 1, if you like it, it won't overly disappoint from there, and it'll retain its fun.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.

Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

The twist at the ending feels a bit forced and lacked foreshadowing for my taste, but I've seen worse.
The gameplay is innovative, but not stellar. You basically drag and drop information highlighted for you in the diverse media you're surveilling. It serves its purpose.
Recommanded for its cautious yet entertaining handling of a important subject!

Orwell simulates the busywork of an office job to tell a larger story about surveillance.

As a game focused on searching through in-game websites for dirt and details, Orwell lives or dies on the strength of its plot and characterization.

The developers of Orwell have done their best to be credible, without being too predictable. The result is that the case you get is not entirely predictable (but that's OK), and the reactions to it surveillance system are credible.

The best thing about Orwell is that it is less cliché than I expected. In the end-game some background was given about it design of the espionage system, and that went deeper than "safety" versus "privacy": they have really thought about it, and have tried to add some sort of ethics. The most annoying aspect is that the system sometimes draws conclusions that are not yours, and there is no button to undo that. That is a completely conscious choice of the developers, but sometimes frustrating for you as a player.

How can one praise a game's writing in a way the Tl;dr preferring masses can understand? Don't know that one can, but I'll leave one at the end anyway! 

In Orwell, you're pulled into a world not unlike our own, on the brink of a massive change, in a country on the edge of totalitarianism. There is intrigue, conspiracy, and secrets, buried, but now possibly revealed by the very same survailance system that threatens the privacy of the nation, and as the investigator wielding it, these secrets may be yours, and yours alone, to witness and discover. What will you do with the knowledge you uncover, with the secrets revealed by your datahunting? Well, that's ultimately up to you. And everything you send to your leaders, and everything you omit, can have consequences, shockingly so, in fact. Even things that seem otherwise innocuous, can bite you in the arse, or even be a saving grace. 
Just remember, lives are in your hands, and it would take multiple playthroughs to truly understand just who is who, and reveal how morally grey these characters are. 
Orwell is a game that has left me lost in thought, and sometimes gazing at my screen in wonder, or even my webcam. Information is power, and Orwell is a narrative to remind your very soul of that fact.

Tl;dr, It's amazing, buy it if you know how to read and like stories where you have the power, and like being forced to make hard choices. And face consequences.
